section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: Reporting guideline for Chatbot Health Advice studies: the CHART statement
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: Design, execution, interpretation, and reporting of economic evaluation studies in obstetrics
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: LETter To the EditoR Standards (LETTERS) : Considerations for Authors, Reviewers, and Editors
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: COMET-Bib: Comprehensive Methodological Transparency for Bibliometric Studies
text:
Bibliometric and scientometric analyses have become indispensable for mapping scientific landscapes, assessing productivity, identifying research gaps, and informing policy and funding strategies. Their relevance extends far beyond information and library sciences, contributing meaningfully to fields such as environmental science, medicine, and climate research, where bibliometric evidence increasingly informs decision-making. By providing this form of “knowledge scaffolding,” bibliometrics not only diagnoses strengths and weaknesses within research systems but also offers a strategic lens on collaboration, impact, and equity.The surge in bibliometric publications is driven by expanding access to databases, the proliferation of user-friendly software platforms, and the integration of artificial intelligence, including large language models, into research workflows. While this has democratised practice, it has also produced wide variation in reporting quality, with many studies privileging data-led outputs over methodological justification.The existing guidelines focus on a comprehensive description of methodology in text but do not provide guidance on presenting a workflow of a bibliometric study, as the PRISMA flow chart does for systematic reviews. The flow charts currently proposed are broad outlines that rely heavily on authors’ creativity, leading to inconsistent reporting. Additionally, PRISMA cannot be used without adaptation, since the workflow of a bibliometric study differs from that of a systematic review.Against this backdrop, a structured and comprehensive reporting guideline is urgently needed. A PRISMA-like framework tailored to bibliometric workflows would enforce methodological rigour, ensure transparent reporting of databases, tools, and analytical steps, and foster interdisciplinary consistency.The proposed guideline “COMET-Bib (Comprehensive Methodological Transparency for Bibliometric Studies)” will address this need. Its scope spans the entire research process: defining research questions, selecting and documenting data sources (e.g., Scopus, Web of Science), applying diverse methodologies (e.g., citation analysis, co-authorship mapping), integrating AI-driven tools for data processing, and presenting results with clarity and reproducibility. COMET-Bib will be designed to accommodate theoretical innovations, applied analyses, and science policy evaluations alike, ensuring relevance across both ILS and non-ILS domains. By promoting transparency, reproducibility, and comparability, COMET-Bib will strengthen bibliometrics as a diagnostic and strategic tool, prevent superficial accumulation of descriptive results, and secure its role as a foundation for advancing knowledge and informing policy.

title: ORIOCE - Guidelines for transparent reporting of Outbreak Reports and Intervention Of Community Epidemics
text:
Outbreak reports offer a timeline-based narrative of methods, findings, and public health responses in active or recently finished outbreaks or public health inquiries. These reports typically encompass the reason for the investigation, symptoms or pathogens involved, time and place of the outbreak, identification of affected individuals, as well as the investigation methods, results, and implications for public health. The ideal structure for these reports is a narrative format that sequentially presents the events. A group of physicians in the Department of Family Medicine Kangdong Sacred Heart Hospital, in South Korea, started developing this reporting guideline for reports of outbreaks of transmissible diseases and the community-level interventions to mitigate them. They have funding from Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency and they plan to publish the guideline, as an open access document, in 2023.

title: TIDIER-A 2026: TIDieR extension for acupuncture: Template for Acupuncture Intervention Description and Replication
text:
Acupuncture is a cornerstone of distinctive Traditional Chinese Medicine therapies and one of the most globally recognized complementary and alternative medicine modalities. With its low cost, ease to operate, and minimal side effects, acupuncture plays an irreplaceable role in primary healthcare, chronic disease management, and geriatric healthcare worldwide.
The key characteristics of acupuncture interventions are individualized treatment and dynamic adjustment. Its effectiveness relies on the synergy of various unique elements, such as acupoint location and needling parameters (needle type, depth, angle, manipulation techniques). However, in current acupuncture research, issues like vague descriptions of interventions, missing information on intervention content, and a lack of standardized reporting have become major obstacles to its advancement. Prof. Tammy C Hoffmann et al. developed reporting guidelines for interventions in 2014, the TIDieR framework lacks the specificity and comprehensive coverage needed for acupuncture research. As a generic intervention reporting framework, it doesn’t include personalized elements crucial to acupuncture, such as precise acupoint location, specific needling techniques, and syndrome differentiation for point selection, making it difficult to address the unique requirements of acupuncture interventions. While the STRICTA guidelines for acupuncture primarily focus on the methodological reporting of acupuncture RCTs, they leave out other types of studies like cohort studies and case reports. Furthermore, STRICTA’s descriptions of acupuncture interventions are often too general and vague, leading to low study reproducibility and making it difficult to replicate findings.
Therefore, we’re developing acupuncture intervention reporting guidelines as a TIDieR extension. Our aim is to address the limitations of the original TIDieR (lack of specificity) and STRICTA (only covering RCTs). We want to provide detailed guidance on acupuncture techniques, improve the quality of acupuncture evidence, provide clinicians with replicable treatment protocols, and facilitate the translation of research findings into clinical practice.

title: Standards for transparent reporting of dental implant studies (STRIDE):
text:
STRIDE (STandards for tRansparent reportIng of Dental Implant studiEs) is a reporting guideline for primary studies evaluating dental implant therapy — surgical placement, prosthodontic loading and restoration, and peri-implant health or disease — whether implant survival/success or peri-implant status is a primary outcome, secondary outcome, or exposure of interest. It is intended for authors, peer reviewers, journal editors, and evidence synthesists across implant dentistry, periodontology, prosthodontics, and oral and maxillofacial surgery. Because implant studies span randomized trials, non-randomized comparative studies, cohort and cross-sectional studies, and case series, STRIDE is deliberately design-transversal rather than tied to a single design.
No existing guideline fills this role. The design-based guidelines CONSORT and STROBE are silent on implant-specific reporting content (implant system and surface, surgical and loading protocol, and which success/survival or peri-implant disease definition was applied), and no CONSORT or STROBE extension for implant dentistry exists or is under development on the EQUATOR register. Two adjacent initiatives sit beside this gap rather than filling it: clinical practice guidelines from ITI, EAO, and AO/AAP consensus workshops recommend what clinicians should do, not what authors should report; and the Implant Dentistry Core Outcome Set and Measurement (ID-COSM; Tonetti et al., 2023) specifies which outcomes implant trials should measure, not how study conduct and those outcomes should be disclosed in a manuscript.
There is empirical evidence that this gap matters. Successive methodological reviews spanning 2011–2025 have found persistent reporting deficiencies specific to implant-dentistry research: incomplete adherence to CONSORT items in implant RCTs (Vere et al., 2011; Cairo et al., 2012), poor reporting quality in implant-RCT abstracts (Menne et al., 2022), inconsistent reporting and methodological quality in split-mouth trials — a design very common in this literature (Qin et al., 2022), inconsistent handling and disclosure of incomplete outcome data such as dropouts and implant failures (Lieber et al., 2020), and gaps in protocol registration and network-geometry reporting in network meta-analyses (Ashi & Khurshid, 2025). Compounding this, implant “success” and “survival” have several competing operational definitions in circulating use since Albrektsson et al. (1986), and peri-implant disease case definitions were only consensus-standardized in 2018 (Berglundh et al.); neither CONSORT nor STROBE requires an author to state which definition was applied, so nominally comparable outcomes across studies may not be measuring the same thing.
STRIDE is therefore conceived as a single, cross-design, evidence-grounded guideline. Its items will be drawn from a scoping review of the implant-dentistry reporting-quality literature and a structured audit of definition use in a corpus of published studies, so that each recommendation addresses a documented, not presumed, reporting deficiency.

title: Reporting Items for Evidence Summary
text:
This reporting guideline is specifically designed for evidence summary articles in the healthcare field. Such articles serve as a vital bridge between research evidence and clinical practice, particularly supporting evidence translation projects and the development of practice guidelines. As a concise form of evidence synthesis, they distill complex research into actionable recommendations to meet the growing clinical demand for efficient knowledge translation. For example, in China, the annual number of published evidence summary articles rose to 311 by 2021, mostly in high-impact journals covering oncology, neurology, and other major clinical fields.Reasons for Developing the New Reporting Guideline1. Methodological inconsistencies in existing practices
Evidence summary articles often lack key methodological details, such as structured research questions, transparent search strategies, and clear evidence grading criteria—weakening their reproducibility and methodological rigor. Meanwhile, the existing “Critical Appraisal for Summaries of Evidence (CASE) tool”, though conceptually relevant, has not been adopted by major journals, leaving a gap in quality evaluation standards.2. Insufficient reporting standardization
Current existing reporting recommendations for evidence summaries include the following aspects: a. JBI Evidence Summary: With rich experience in developing rapid review and evidence summary methodologies, JBI aims to complete evidence summaries within a week, using a fixed 6-part structure (title, question, clinical bottom line, characteristics of the Evidence, best practice recommendations, references). b. Critically Appraised Topic (CAT): Organized around clinical questions, CAT provides both research appraisal and clinical relevance explanations. It follows 5 steps of evidence-based practice (EBP): “Ask, Search, Appraise, Apply, Evaluate”. c. Framework by Weijie Xing (Fudan University): Derived from analyzing domestic and international evidence summaries, it includes 5 sections (background, methods, results, discussion, Summary).However, these frameworks only outline overall structures without specifying details of each reporting item. Moreover, their development did not follow the methodological guidelines for reporting standard formulation recommended by the EQUATOR Network. Additionally, key information is often missing—such as unclear basis for recommendation strength, undisclosed conflict-of-interest statements, and inadequate documentation of evidence integration methods—hindering readers’ assessment of research credibility and applicability.Escalating needs for practice and translation As foundational inputs for clinical practice innovations and intervention development, poorly reported evidence summaries may lead to risks like misleading practice changes or suboptimal protocol design

title: TARGET-TCM: a reporting guideline extension of the TARGET Statement for traditional Chinese medicine
text:
TARGET-TCM is a proposed extension of the TARGET (Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial) Statement for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) interventions. It will apply to studies of Chinese herbal medicines, Chinese patent medicines, acupuncture and other TCM non-pharmacological interventions, integrated Chinese and Western medicine, and syndrome-based or dynamically individualized treatment strategies.
The original TARGET Statement provides a general framework for transparent reporting of causal questions, target trial specifications, emulation using observational data, identification assumptions, statistical analyses, results, and limitations. However, TCM studies involve reporting challenges that may not be fully captured by the original checklist. These include defining and operationalizing TCM syndromes and constitutions; representing individualized and dynamically modified treatments; standardizing herbal formulas, modified prescriptions, and treatment-strategy families; specifying timing, duration, interruption, and sequencing of combined Chinese and Western medicine; aligning syndrome differentiation, prescribing, dispensing, treatment initiation, and time zero; addressing time-varying treatment and confounding; and reporting TCM-specific outcomes and data quality.
TARGET-TCM will retain the structure and principles of TARGET while clarifying, extending, or adding items only where TCM-specific information is needed for reproducibility, risk-of-bias appraisal, causal interpretation, and appropriate delineation of the evidence boundary. It is intended as a reporting guideline, not as a methodological guideline prescribing how target trial emulation studies must be conducted.

title: COREMILK: COnsensus Guidelines for REsearch on Human MILK
text:
Human milk research is an expanding and critical field with important implications for maternal and infant health, yet methodological reporting across human milk composition studies is highly variable and frequently incomplete. The proposed reporting guideline, COREMILK (COnsensus Guidelines for REsearch on Human MILK), will provide a standardized framework for reporting research focused on human milk composition analysis.
This guideline will apply to studies investigating any component of human milk (macronutrients, micronutrients, bioactives, microbiota, contaminants, and other constituents) across different populations and contexts. It will cover observational studies, interventional studies, and method development or validation studies involving analysis of human milk composition. COREMILK will specify minimum essential reporting standards across several key domains, including participant demographics, lactation and feeding practices, milk sample collection, handling and storage methods, analytical procedures, and statistical reporting.
A new reporting guideline is urgently needed to address significant inconsistencies in current reporting practices. Critical methodological factors - such as sampling time postpartum, collection technique (hand expression vs. pumping), milk fraction analysed (whole vs. skim), and analytical validation details - are often inadequately described or omitted entirely. These omissions impair reproducibility, prevent robust meta-analyses, and limit the translation of findings into clinical and public health practice. Existing general reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT, STROBE) are not tailored to the unique challenges of human milk research and thus cannot fully meet the field’s needs.
By establishing consensus-based reporting standards, COREMILK will strengthen the transparency, comparability, and interpretability of human milk composition research. The guideline is intended to support researchers, reviewers, editors, and funders in improving research quality and accelerating progress in this vital area of maternal and child health science.

title: WHO Trial Registration Data Set (TRDS) extension for organoid studies
text:
Organoids are 3D in vitro structures derived from stem cells that recapitulate the cellular heterogeneity, architecture, and function of human organs. They have been widely used in preclinical and early clinical research, however, organoid trials have unique features distinct from conventional clinical trials, such as organoid derivation, culture, characterization, quality control, and intervention administration.
At present, the WHO Trial Registration Data Set (TRDS) does not cover these organoid‑specific items, leading to incomplete, inconsistent, and non‑transparent registration of organoid trials worldwide. Poor registration hinders study reproducibility, peer review, clinical translation, and public trust.
To address this gap, we propose to develop the WHO TRDS extension for organoid, a reporting checklist tailored to organoid‑related clinical trials.
In this guideline, organoid clinical research is defined as observational or experimental studies that use human biological samples (healthy or patient-derived tissues, cells, blood, etc.) to construct organoids, with the core goal of addressing clinical disease-related questions. This definition explicitly includes in vitro studies using human-derived materials, which may not be regarded as clinical research under conventional definitions. Based on research purpose and application scenario, organoid clinical research is further categorized into six core types: (1) drug sensitivity testing / drug screening; (2) disease modeling; (3) disease diagnosis; (4) database construction; (5) disease treatment; and (6) regenerative medicine /organoid transplantation.
This extension will supplement organoid‑specific registration items while remaining compatible with the core WHO TRDS framework. It will improve the completeness, transparency, and quality of organoid trial registration, support evidence synthesis and clinical translation, and promote the rigorous and sustainable development of organoid medicine globally.

title: REFORH: REporting guideline For ORganoids in Human clinical studies
text:
Organoids are three-dimensional structures derived from pluripotent stem cells, adult stem cells, or primary somatic cells, and retain key histological, molecular, and genetic features of their tissue of origin. In recent years, organoid technologies have increasingly been incorporated into human clinical studies, including studies in which patient-derived organoids are generated from clinical samples and used to investigate clinical response patterns, drug sensitivity, or associations between organoid-based readouts and patient-level clinical characteristics or outcomes. Moreover, organoid models align with the “3Rs” principle—Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement— and are increasingly explored as human-relevant experimental systems that may complement traditional animal-based approaches. Recent regulatory initiatives, including those from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, have acknowledged the potential role of organoid-based and other in vitro methods as part of New Approach Methodologies aimed at reducing reliance on animal testing in drug development and translational research contexts.The increasing number of organoid-related clinical studies in recent years further underscores the need to establish a reporting guideline. As interest in organoid-based clinical research continues to grow, so does the demand for standardized reporting guidelines.However, no dedicated reporting framework currently exists for organoid-based clinical studies, increasing the risk of incomplete reporting and the prevalence of selective interpretation of findings. For example, clinical studies involving organoids typically require reporting on the organoid’s composition, source, derivation, and key experimental or analytical procedures. However, existing reporting guidelines for clinical research, such as CONSORT for randomized trials and STROBE for observational studies, do not include items addressing these organoid-specific considerations.Therefore, the project leads advocate for the development of a reporting guideline specific to organoid clinical studies. Such a guideline would not only improve the quality and transparency of organoid research reporting but also facilitate the translation of basic science into clinical applications, ultimately accelerating the advancement of personalized medicine and interdisciplinary innovation.

title: CheRIHoSS - Checklist of Reporting Items for Horizon Scanning Studies
text:
Horizon scanning is a method used to systematically detect signs of future developments. In health and care is it used to inform decisions about new and emergining innovative health and care technologies before these technologies become available and evidence is generated. The use of horizon scanning in health and care decision-making is gaining traction. Current applications of horizon scanning in the health and care context include: predicting the impact of new technologies on health and care services, regulatory frameworks or policies; identifying future developments, gaps, trends or business opportunities; and helping with adoption and diffusion of new technologies. Furthermore, horizon scanning is already established as a crucial step in the health technology assessment (HTA) process as a method to detect innovative technologies and issue early alerts to HTA bodies ahead of these technologies being placed on the market. There are other multiple uses and applications of horizon scanning methods in the healthcare context. This variability and broad application warrant the need for transparent and robust methods reporting. Currently there is an absence of guidelines for reporting the methods used in these studies. A lack of clear standardised terminology also means that study methods are often unclear.This guideline aims to fill the methodological gap identified by providing a checklist and a glossary of terms that horizon scanning practitioners, researchers, peer-reviewers and journal editors can work with to improve quality and consistency of horizon scanning studies.This guideline and checklist is the result of years of practice in the field of horizon scanning in health and care.

title: APT-SAP: Enhancing the design, conduct and analysis of Adaptive and Platform Trials through consensus-driven Statistical Analysis Plan guidance
text:
The increasing need for efficient and innovative trial designs to rapidly evaluate investigative treatments and expedite clinical decision-making for the quick benefit of patients has led to the growing use of Adaptive and Platform Trials (APTs) in a randomised setting. Adaptive designs allow for pre-specified changes to trial design aspects (trial adaptations) based on accrued interim outcome data while maintaining valid conclusions. Examples of trial adaptations include early stopping of ineffective treatment arms, early trial stopping upon gathering sufficient evidence to reach conclusions, or allocating more participants to promising treatment arms. Platform trials further enhance this flexibility by enabling the addition of new treatment arms (or study populations/subpopulations) to an ongoing study, with or without interim analyses.
While APTs offer clear benefits, their inherent flexibility and statistical efficiency introduce considerable operational and statistical complexities across the design, conduct, analysis, and reporting stages. Trial adaptations should be accounted for in all these stages to yield valid, trustworthy, and interpretable results, and to maintain public confidence in the generated evidence. Therefore, timely access to high-quality Statistical Analysis Plans (SAPs) for APTs, addressing both interim and final analyses alongside detailed protocols, is vital for enhancing transparency and facilitating accurate interpretation of results.
However, current SAP guidance does not adequately address the specific considerations posed by APTs in randomised setting. Many publicly available APT-SAPs, including related reports of published results, provide insufficient detail on statistical methods. This makes it difficult to interpret reported results and reproduce methods and findings – hindering the credibility of reported results. This lack of transparency undermines public trust and contributes to research waste. In addition, there is a notable absence of guidance on the proportionate level of interim information that can be released (e.g., to trial participants, patients, investigators, or the research community at conferences) from ongoing APTs without compromising trial integrity.

title: Standards for transparent reporting of aligner treatment studies (STRAND)
text:
STRAND (STandards for tRansparent reporting of Aligner treatmeNt stuDies) is a reporting guideline for primary studies evaluating clear aligner therapy — tooth movement accuracy and predictability, treatment duration and efficiency, compliance, retention, and comparative effectiveness against fixed appliances — across randomized trials, retrospective and prospective cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and case series. It is intended for authors, peer reviewers, journal editors, and evidence synthesists in orthodontics and dentofacial orthopedics. Because clear aligner studies span multiple designs rather than concentrating in one, STRAND is deliberately design-transversal.
No existing guideline fills this role. CONSORT’s orthodontic-trial adaptation (Pandis et al., 2015) is appliance-neutral and RCT-only, and most aligner studies are not RCTs. STROBE is silent on appliance-specific content. OHStat (Best et al., 2024), a recent discipline-agnostic guideline for oral health observational studies and trials, incorporates STROBE and CONSORT generically but by design cannot name aligner-specific items — brand, attachment protocol, staging, compliance-monitoring method — any more than it names implant- or endodontic-specific items. A 2025 international Delphi consensus on clear aligner treatment (Arveda et al., AJODO) is a clinical-practice document — what aligners can and cannot clinically achieve — not a reporting guideline, and does not address manuscript disclosure.
There is empirical evidence that this gap matters. Robertson et al. (2020) found that of 7 eligible primary studies on aligner effectiveness, only 1 was an RCT and 6 were retrospective cohorts, with 6 of 7 judged moderate risk of bias and 1 high. Bichu et al. (2024) found that current aligner research literature “fails to standardize or report” malocclusion severity, aligner brand, material properties, patient compliance, and total aligner count, and that protocol variation in aligner-change timing goes undisclosed — naming, in effect, a ready-made list of candidate reporting items. Reflecting these weaknesses, a synthesis of 18 systematic reviews of aligner predictability found none achieved high AMSTAR-2 quality and only 3 reached moderate, a limitation traceable to the primary literature underneath. Independently, critical commentary on the 2025 Delphi consensus flagged continued reliance on low-quality retrospective evidence in the field.
STRAND is therefore conceived as a single, cross-design, evidence-grounded guideline sitting on top of the generic scaffolds already in use (OHStat, STROBE, CONSORT), adding the disclosure items specific to clear aligner therapy. Its items will be drawn from a scoping review of the aligner reporting-quality literature, so that each recommendation addresses a documented, not presumed, deficiency.

title: Reporting checklist for systematic review of clinical practice guidelines: a RIGHT extension statement
text:
Scientific reporting of clinical practice guidelines helps promote the completeness, transparency, and reliability of guidelines. The current existence of multiple clinical practice guidelines in a particular field or for a particular disease at the same time calls for a systematic review of these guidelines to analyse their methodological quality, quality of reporting, quality of the evidence and the direction, strength and content of the recommendations, investigative analysis of a particular part of the guideline. Currently, systematic reviews of clinical practice guidelines are widely published, but a reporting checklist of such systematic reviews is lacking. Therefore, we drew on the RIGHT, PRISMA, and MOOSE checklist development process and on the standardized production steps provided by the EQUAOR Collaborative Network to develop the SCREEN (reporting checklist for SystematiC Review of clinical practicE guidEliNes) checklist with a view to providing a useful tool for better reporting of systematic reviews of clinical practice guidelines.
The development of RIGHT for SCREEN has received support from Pro. Yaolong Chen, the initiator of the RIGHT statement, as a co-initiator, providing methodological guidance for the development of the extension version of RIGHT for SCREEN.

title: CGM-REPORT: A Reporting Guideline for Studies Using Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Individuals Without Diabetes
text:
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is increasingly used in research involving individuals without diagnosed diabetes, including populations with normoglycemia, prediabetes, metabolic risk, and other non-diabetic conditions. However, substantial variability exists in the reporting of CGM methodology and outcomes, including participant and glycemic-status definitions, CGM device characteristics, monitoring duration and data completeness, sensor wear and visibility, data processing, metric definitions, glucose thresholds, and calculation methods. Incomplete or inconsistent reporting can limit reproducibility, comparability across studies, interpretation of findings, and quantitative evidence synthesis.
CGM-REPORT aims to develop an evidence- and consensus-based reporting guideline defining the minimum information that should be reported in studies using CGM in individuals without diagnosed diabetes. The guideline is intended to be applicable across relevant research designs in which CGM data are collected or analysed, rather than being restricted to a single clinical condition, CGM metric, or study design. It will complement existing study-design-specific reporting guidelines by providing CGM-specific reporting items that are not sufficiently addressed by general reporting frameworks.
The initial candidate reporting items will be informed by an empirical assessment of reporting practices and deficiencies identified through our ongoing systematic review and meta-analysis of CGM reference values in individuals without diabetes, together with existing reporting guidelines and relevant CGM guidance. Candidate items will subsequently be refined through a structured international multidisciplinary consensus process. The resulting guideline is intended to improve the transparency, completeness, reproducibility, and comparability of CGM research in individuals without diabetes and to facilitate interpretation, replication, evidence synthesis, and future clinical translation. title: Psychological self-Report Instruments in Databases: the PRIDE Reporting Guideline
text:
The proliferation of psychological databases worldwide has created an unprecedented opportunity for secondary data analysis using self-reported psychological assessments. Countries across the globe have established comprehensive databases containing psychological modules, including the UK Biobank, the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) covering 20 European countries, the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), China’s CHARLS(The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study), and emerging databases in resource-limited settings such as maternal health databases along the Myanmar-Thailand border. These databases predominantly rely on self-reported assessment tools to capture psychological data, generating a substantial volume of research publications indexed in PubMed and Web of Science that utilize secondary psychological self-assessment data.
However, this rapid growth in database-driven psychological research has revealed significant reporting gaps that distinguish these studies from traditional primary data collection observational studies. Research utilizing secondary psychological self-assessment database data presents unique methodological challenges that require specialized reporting considerations. The reliance on pre-existing self-reported assessment tools introduces complexities regarding the validation and applicability of these instruments when applied to secondary database populations that may differ substantially from the original validation cohorts.
Several critical reporting elements are consistently underreported in current literature. For self-assessment tools, particularly psychological scales, studies frequently fail to adequately report the reliability and validity evidence, the source and appropriateness of cutoff points, and whether these parameters were derived from the secondary database population or transferred from original literature populations. Database-specific methodological issues, such as approaches to handling bias when required covariates are unavailable in existing database variables, are often inadequately addressed. Additionally, psychological research, even in general population studies, requires reporting of population-specific contextual factors that may serve as confounders, including pandemic effects, addictive behaviors, and other psychological stressors that may not be routinely captured in standard epidemiological reporting.
Currently, researchers in this field predominantly rely on general observational reporting frameworks such as STROBE. While these frameworks provide a useful foundation for observational research, they do not adequately address the specific methodological considerations involved in studies using psychological self-report instruments in large databases, particularly regarding the reporting of instrument validity, reliability, and the generalizability of findings derived from secondary data. This gap has resulted in inconsistent and often insufficient reporting of critical methodological details, limiting the ability of readers to assess study quality, replicate findings, and synthesize evidence across studies. The PRIDE reporting guideline aims to address these gaps by providing structured guidance for reporting studies using psychological self-report instruments in large databases.

title: Reporting Guidelines for drug utilization and pharmacoepidemiological studies using the WHO ATC/DDD methodoloogy: the EMMA checklist
text:
The ATC/DDD classification system is a global standard endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and is widely used for drug utilization and pharmacoepidemiological research. The Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification allows the classification and retrieval of medicinal substances according to a five-level hierarchy. The Defined Daily Dose (DDD) represents a standard unit of measure of drug consumption. The amount of active substance, pharmaceutical product, or the number of dosage units corresponding to 1 DDD is specific for each ATC 5th-level code (for some ATC 5th-level code a different DDD is assigned to each route of administration), and is established by the WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology (WHO-CC), which also updates the ATC/DDD index annually. Currently, DDDs have been established for most, but not all, of the ATC 5th-level codes. Sometimes, a provisional DDD might be assigned locally for drug consumption monitoring to obtain full coverage of national ATC-based data collection systems. The practical implementation of the ATC/DDD system relies on the correct linkage between ATC codes and the corresponding active substances contained in medicinal product packages. The linkage between an ATC code and a medicinal product package also allows calculation of the ‘number’ of DDDs per package (DPP), a widely used measure of drug consumption often used as a proxy for the number of days’ supply. The implementation and maintenance of the ATC/DDD system may be prone to human error and/or local variations in the application of the WHO guidelines. To reduce possible misalignment in the implementation and maintenance of the ATC/DDD standard, the WHO recommends that one trained centre in each country should be responsible for linking the national medicinal product package dictionary to the most updated release of the ATC/DDD index, as well as for calculating the DPP. Indeed, divergent ATC/DDD versions, differences in the assignment of ATC codes and/or DDDs for combination products, and the use of unofficial or national DDDs were documented as methodological problems that can hamper comparability and reproducibility of studies across countries.
In this context, the quality of reporting practices in pharmacoepidemiological research using the ATC/DDD methodology is fundamental to ensuring transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of studies. However, no explicit recommendations for reporting the use of the ATC/DDD methodology to construct study variables are available in current reporting guidelines for the execution of drug utilisation and pharmacoepidemiological studies, neither in RECORD-PE nor STaRT-RWE.
The aim of this study is to develop recommendations on reporting practices and a checklist for studies using the ATC/DDD methodology for drug utilization and pharmacoepidemiological research intended to be used as an extension of existing reporting guidelines for observationa studies.

title: The Readability Checklist: A reporting guideline for studies assessing the readability of written health information
text:
The Readability Checklist provides a set of recommendations that should be included in studies assessing the readability of written health information. Its primary purpose is to improve methodological rigor, transparency, and reproducibility in this growing area of research.
Readability assessment is the most common used approach to revise and evaluate written health information. With the proliferation of readability formulas and automated tools, studies assessing readability have increased substantially across diverse health domains. However, recent reviews highlight significant variability in reporting practices, including incomplete descriptions of methods, lack of justification for formula and calculator selection, and insufficient detail on text preparation and analysis. These gaps hinder meaningful comparison across studies and limit the ability to replicate findings.
The need for this guideline was reinforced by our recent eDelphi study (under review), which sought to identify and gain consensus on research priorities in order to determine the role of readability assessment in health literate document design. One of the key priorities was the need to establish best practices for conducting and reporting readability analyses. Currently, no standardized reporting framework exists for this type of research. As a result, studies often omit critical information which may compromise transparency and lead to misinterpretation of results. The Readability Checklist addresses these issues by outlining essential reporting items for studies assessing readability of health information. It is intended for researchers, health information developers, journal editors, and peer reviewers. By promoting consistent and comprehensive reporting, the guideline aims to enhance the quality of evidence and improve methodological rigour and reporting transparency.

title: M-TRAIN REPORT: Reporting Guideline for Simulation-Based Training, Education and Research in Medical and Health Care
text:
The SIM-TRAIN REPORT guideline aims to standardize the reporting of simulation-based training, education, and research across the medical and health professions, including medicine, pharmacy, nursing, dentistry, and allied health disciplines. It will be applicable to a broad range of simulation modalities, including high- and low-fidelity simulation, standardized/simulated patients, task trainers, virtual simulation, augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR), serious games, and artificial intelligence-assisted simulation. Simulation is increasingly used not only for knowledge and skills development, clinical reasoning, communication, teamwork, patient safety, competency assessment, and continuing professional development, but also as a research methodology and controlled environment for investigating clinical, educational, behavioral, human-factor, and healthcare-system questions. Despite its expanding role, reporting remains inconsistent. Published studies may omit essential information about the research or educational context, objectives, study and scenario design, simulation modality and fidelity, participant characteristics and preparation, facilitator or researcher roles, prebriefing, debriefing, technology and equipment, data collection procedures, assessment methods, outcome measures, implementation procedures, and resources required for replication.
Incomplete reporting limits critical appraisal, reproducibility, comparison across studies and settings, evidence synthesis, and translation of simulation findings into education and practice. General reporting guidelines such as CONSORT, STROBE, and TIDieR address important methodological elements but are not specifically designed to capture the educational, research, operational, and technological characteristics of simulation-based activities. SIM-TRAIN REPORT will therefore provide a structured, multidisciplinary reporting framework covering the research and educational context, study objectives and design, simulation intervention and scenario, participants, learners, facilitators and researchers, prebriefing and debriefing, data collection, assessment and outcomes, technology and equipment, ethics and safety, implementation, and reproducibility. The guideline is intended for researchers, educators, clinicians, simulation professionals, journal editors, reviewers, and institutions reporting simulation-based training, education, and research in the medical, health care and patient care fields.

title: The CLAIRE statement: a comprehensive reporting and assessing guideline for artificial intelligence in diagnostic imaging
text:
Based on literature reviews and prior experience, numerous inconsistencies have been identified in the reporting of diagnostic imaging studies, especially within dental radiology. Recognising that these same concerns apply broadly across all medical imaging, a new framework is urgently required. Existing tools such as CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI distinguish themselves by narrow orientations centred on trials or protocols, often lacking the architectural depth to encompass the entire diagnostic workflow. The “Completeness, Learnability, Applicability, Interpretability, Reproducibility, and Evaluation” (CLAIRE) framework aims to bridge this gap. It is presented in three components: (i) a table detailing the importance of each featured concept, (ii) a checklist, and (iii) a grading score to assess the overall reporting quality of a manuscript. CLAIRE seamlessly integrates methodological rigour with real world clinical relevance. It operationalises its six core principles into a unified checklist that uniquely mandates the disclosure of raw results for critical appraisal and heavily emphasises interpretability for clinicians who are not experts in the field. Furthermore, by incorporating an objective scoring system, CLAIRE transcends basic reporting to provide a reproducible assessment tool for journal editors and peer reviewers, effectively bridging the gap between technical artificial intelligence development and safe, transparent clinical application.

title: A reporting guideline for the use of artificial intelligence in legal research: reporting standards for legal research in which generative artificial intelligence or large language models are used
text:
This guideline will specify the minimum information that authors should report when artificial intelligence, and in particular generative artificial intelligence and large language models, has been used in the conduct of legal research. It is intended to apply to legal scholarship generally, including doctrinal analysis and empirical legal studies, and to the use of both general-purpose models and AI-enabled commercial legal research platforms. It addresses AI used as an instrument of the research rather than AI as the object of study.
Reporting guidelines addressing artificial intelligence now exist across the health and behavioural sciences, including GUIDE-LLM for large language models in the behavioural and social sciences, and PRISMA-trAIce for AI used as a tool within evidence synthesis. No equivalent guidance exists for legal research, and the guidelines developed in other disciplines do not address the reporting problems that are distinctive to law.
Legal scholarship depends on the accurate identification, citation and characterisation of primary authority. Generative AI systems are known to fabricate case citations, to misdescribe the holdings of decisions that do exist, and to blend jurisdictions. Authority may be genuine and accurately described and nonetheless be from the wrong jurisdiction, no longer good law, or not binding on the question addressed. None of the existing AI reporting guidelines contains items directed to any of these problems, because they do not arise in the same form outside law. Similarly, no existing guideline addresses whether a model or platform has been adapted for the jurisdiction whose law is being researched, what corpus of authority it was able to search, or whether it was used for interpretive tasks such as identifying the ratio of a decision, determining whether authority is binding or persuasive, or applying principles of statutory interpretation.
Guidance that does exist for law is fragmented and was not designed for scholarship. Courts in several jurisdictions have issued practice directions requiring the verification of cited authority and restricting the entry of privileged or suppressed material into AI tools, but these govern the conduct of litigation, and the leading Australian practice note expressly excludes dedicated AI legal research software from its operation. Law journals and law reviews have adopted policies that differ as to what triggers disclosure, what must be disclosed, and where the disclosure should appear, and a recent survey of United States law journals found that most have no formal policy at all. The consequence is that legal researchers have no settled standard to report against, readers and editors have no consistent basis on which to appraise AI-assisted legal scholarship, and journals have no developed instrument to adopt. Because legal scholarship is used by courts, law reform bodies and policy makers, the consequences of unreliable or unappraisable work extend beyond the academy. This guideline will fill that gap through a formal consensus process conducted in accordance with EQUATOR Network guidance.

title: Transparent Reporting of Adaptations, Context, and Effects
text:

Systematic reviews and meta-analysis have shown the importance of adapting interventions to increase the reach and retention of historically and currently marginalized populations in clinical and implementation science trials. Additionally, the field of adaptation has indicated that there may be adaptations needed as interventions are implemented and then sustained in usual care. Despite the plethora of frameworks informing how to adapt, when to adapt, and how to track adaptations made to interventions, systematic, narrative and scoping reviews – along with our recent ongoing review – show that there is no consistency in reporting in adaptation studies. When there is inconsistency in reporting of study methods and outcomes, it affects replication of science and understanding of mechanisms of change of the interventions being adapted. To address this gap, we will develop reporting guidelines for adaptation studies.

title: AGREE II Extension for Reporting of Guidelines in Surgery – AGREE-S
text:

Using statistical models, they have developed and published an evaluation of 67 existing guidelines in 2020 (GAP II). Furthermore, they conducted a Delphi process of a panel of stakeholders (GAP III) to inform the development of the extension document. The executive group discussed the results of the three parts of the project and finalised the document in a consensus meeting in September 2021. title: The RAPPORT Statement: Reporting Guideline for Rigor and Reproducibility in Community-engaged research
text:
The National Institutes of Health in the United States recently issued guidance that all funded science and studies must be rigorus and reproducable. However, there is a natural tension between community-engaged work and the current way scientific standards define rigor and reproducibility. For example, repeated measures make a study more rigorous, but may increase community burden and a study done in one community will likely need to be tailored before being repeated, which may be viewed as being less reproducable.
While interest in Community-Engaged Research continues to grow those designing and publishing studies often fail to describe how partnerships were formed, how decisions were shared, or how methods were carried out. Without that information, readers and reviewers cannot judge a study’s rigor, replicate its approach, or compare findings across studies.
Purpose: RAPPORT gives authors, reviewers, and editors a common standard for reporting CEnR. Its goal is to make both the engagement process and the research methods transparent, auditable, and reproducible, while respecting community ownership and context.
The RAPPORT Domains:

Rigor: Describe the study design, the rationale for engagement methods, and the strategies used to ensure the study is credible and valid.
Accountability: Report how researchers and community partners were accountable to each other, including agreements, conflict resolution, and responsiveness to community feedback.
Partnership: Identify community partners, how they were recruited, the history of the relationship, and the resources and compensation given to them.
Participation: Specify the level and timing of community involvement at each research stage, from question development to dissemination.
Openness: Disclose governance, power sharing, data ownership, and any limits on data or material sharing agreed with communities.

Reproducibility: Give enough detail on engagement and research procedures for others to adapt or replicate them, including protocols, tools, and analytic decisions.

Transparency: Report deviations from plans, limitations, conflicts of interest, and how results were returned to communities.

Scope: RAPPORT applies to quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods Community-Engaged Research (CEnR), including community-based participatory research (CBPR) done in collaboration with community and Community Partnered Participatory Research (CPPR). We do not believe this guideline currently exists in EQUATOR, and this is meant to complement existing EQUATOR guidelines such GRIPP2, not replace them. However, we note that GRIPP2 has related concepts, are open to considering an extension.
We note that RAPPORT is not for patients (which is a different dynamic) nor is it for “the public”, it is specific to community engaged and co-lead research techniques which may include may types of study design.
Use: Authors can use RAPPORT when planning, writing, and submitting manuscripts. Reviewers and editors can use it to appraise how completely CEnR is reported, and researchers can use it to assess rigor and reproducibility across the published CEnR literature.

title: PRISMA-EE - PRISMA guideline extension for systematic reviews of health economic evaluations
text:
Systematic reviews of health economic evaluations consider health economic evaluations, which compare the effects of different healthcare interventions on economic outcomes (e.g. incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, incremental benefits, etc). However, these reviews, albeit common, have varied quality standards of reporting.
A group based in the University of Oxford, with PRISMA representatives, is leading this project of developing a reporting guideline for systematic reviews of health economic evaluations. A working group is being formed, and the leaders plan to perform a scoping review of the methodological literature, a Delphi survey, a consensus meeting, and piloting before launching. The project has funding from NIHR, and the group plans to publish the reporting guideline in 2026, as an open-access document.

title: RECONSIDER – Reporting extension of CONSORT and SPIRIT for Inclusion, Diversity, Ethnicity and Race
text:
This project to develop an extension of CONSORT and SPIRIT reporting guidelines will focus on the reporting of variables relevant to ethnically, culturally and linguistically diverse participants in randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The resulting guideline will cover both methodological (for example, techniques of recuitment) and reporting aspects (relevant data for ethnically diverse people) of RCTs and will apply to both the main manuscript and supplementary materials.
The leading group plans to review the literature, consult with diverse ethnic communities in Australia, UK and Canada and conduct a Delphi survey. The development of the project, funded by the Commonwealth of Australia (represented by the National Health and Medical Research Council) started in February 2022, and the group plans to publish the guideline as an open-access document.

title: Blinding in Acupuncture Clinical Trials: guidelines for assessment and reporting
text:
Placebo effects and patient expectations can significantly influence outcomes of acupuncture treatment. The leaders of this project consider CONSORT, a guideline for clinical trials, insufficient to adequately guide the reporting of the implementation of blinding procedures in acupuncture trials. They propose to develop a guideline that will support authors on reporting these procedures, and possibly help with their evaluation as well. According to the project leaders, “This guideline will provide clear instructions on how to report the methods and results of blinding procedures, including the assessment of blinding success and the comprehensive and transparent reports of blinding . The scope of the guideline will encompass the entire process of trial design, from the initial designing stages through to the final reporting of results.”
They plan to develop the guideline first establishing the project team, which will not include members of the public (patients). A Delphi survey is planned, as well as an expert consensus meeting and a pre-test of the checklist. The authors declare they have funding for the project from High-level Talent Programme of Beijing University of Chinese Medicine. They plan to publish the reporting guideline as an open-access document in 2027.

title: EPIC - Enhanced Prevalence and Incidence Criteria
text:
The lack of standardisation in reports on the prevalence and incidence of diseases and other health-related events inspired a group of international experts on infectious diseases, epidemiology and modelling to meet in December 2022. At the meeting, the participants agreed that there was a considerable need for a STROBE guideline extension for observational studies of the prevalence and incidence of infectious and non-communicable diseases.
The core executive group aims to develop an extension of STROBE, for which they are trying to contact-STROBE authors for collaboration.
They already conducted a Delphi exercise including 31 international experts on a preliminary checklist; 22 of whom were present in a face-to-face consensus meeting in South Africa on 6 December 2022. Participants discussed and reached a consensus on the rationale for including items in the checklist, developed a flow diagram and the strategy for producing documents, decided who would be involved in which activities, authorship, and knowledge translation strategy, and generated an early version of the checklist. They are now preparing to conduct the second Delphi exercise, and they plan to pilot-test the checklist. The work receives funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation through the University of Maryland. The group plans to publish the reporting guideline in 2024 as an open-access paper.

title: CARITS - Complete and Accurate Reporting of Interrupted Time Series studies
text:
Interrupted time series (ITS) designs are commonly used to evaluate the effects of interventions targeted at populations (for example, changes to public health policy) or the impacts of exposures (such as natural disasters). In an ITS, a series of observations are collected both before and after an interruption. The impact of the interruption can then be quantified by comparing the observed post-interruption trend with the counterfactual. The design is less susceptible to bias than some other non-randomised designs (such as before-after design) and can be strengthened by the addition of control series. Complete and accurate reporting of the design and statistical methods is required so that readers can understand, for example, the details of the interruption(s), features of the design (e.g. number of periods, number of data points), the structure of the fitted model, statistical methods, and the effect measures used to quantify the interruption’s impact. A number of studies examining the methods of ITS studies have identified incomplete reporting of key design and statistical details.
The core group developing this reporting guideline is primarily based at the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine at Monash University. They received funding from the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) to develop a reporting guideline for ITS studies.
The group plans to publish a protocol including literature reviews, surveys with stakeholders, and a face-to-face consensus meeting. They plan to publish their reporting guideline as an explanation and elaboration open-access document around 2025-6.

title: PRISMA-P Update - Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols
text:
PRISMA-P (“PRISMA for protocols”) was initially published in 2015. Since then, the field of systematic reviews and meta-analyses has expanded, new methodological and reporting practices have evolved, and the role of protocols in clinical research has been increasingly debated. The original PRISMA guideline from 2009 for completed systematic reviews was-updated and published as PRISMA 2020.
The PRISMA-P 2025 steering group plans to update the reporting guideline for protocols for systematic reviews, harmonising it with PRISMA 2020. The PRISMA-P 2025 will provide guidance for the minimum content necessary for the protocol of a systematic review.
The update will be developed in six stages:

reviews - supporting projects including a scoping review identifying published comments and suggestions for modifications on PRISMA-P 2015, and an empirical study analysing the adherence to PRISMA-P 2015 among systematic review protocols stating to have used the reporting guideline
draft - using the existing PRISMA-P 2015 reporting guideline as a starting point, an initial draft of guideline items will be developed based on the evidence identified in the supporting projects together with items included in PRISMA 2020 and relevant PRISMA extensions.
survey - an online survey among a large international survey panel to help decide on items that could be modified, added to, or removed from PRISMA-P 2015
refinement - a consensus meeting with an advisory group
write-up - drafting the-updated list of items
publication - two manuscripts: the PRISMA-P 2025 guideline statement and the explanation and elaboration (E&E) document.

The study protocol is under development, and no funding was obtained so far. The leaders plan to publish the update as an open access document.

title: Minimum standards for content and format of meta-data and data reporting in systematic reviews
text:
Reporting transparency many times involves making available sets of data that are related to the main research report. The way these materials are uploaded to online platforms interferes with the discoverability by systematic reviewers. With that in mind, this group is proposing a guideline with a list of minimum requirements for the formatting of files, especially regarding meta-data, to allow machine readability and reuse. They plan to set standards for the reporting of all decisions taken during the study retrieval, selection, data extraction, and critical appraisal processes of a systematic review. For the description of the content and format, they want to be able to specify the file format (e.g. .txt, .ris, .csv, .json as opposed to .pdf, .docx., or .accdb) and the internal structure of the document (e.g. field tags for .ris formats, which field tag should contain eligibility decision tags at each level of screening). A longer-term aim is to encourage that data to have doi numbers and are freely accessible (FAIR/Open Data) through data archiving.
The guidance will apply to all systematic reviews, irrespective of the discipline, including reviews in sustainability, climate change, healthcare, international development, environmental science, social welfare, etc.
The group is planning a Delphi-style process and a future multidisciplinary expert panel to reach a consensus.

title: SPIRIT-ROUTINE - for protocols of trials using cohorts and routinely collected data
text:
The reporting guideline SPIRIT guides the reporting of protocols of clinical trials. This project aims to systematically develop, test and effectively disseminate an extension of SPIRIT specifically for studies conducted using cohorts and routinely collected data (RCD): the SPIRIT-ROUTINE. The project comprises five stages: 1- project launch, steering group gathering and definition of the scope of the extension; 2 - rapid literature review including other key reporting guidelines; 3 - two-round Delphi exercise; 4 - virtual consensus meeting that will finalise the items to include in the extension; 5 - publication preparation and dissemination of the final checklist. The group plans to publish the project protocol soon. The final publication of the reporting guideline is planned as an open-access document.

title: Standards of Reporting the Network Pharmacology of Chinese Medicine
text:
Since 2010, the concepts and methods of network pharmacology have been applied in traditional Chinese medicine research, and they have played a significant role in identifying potential herbal therapies during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2021, Li Shao developed the “Guidelines for Network Pharmacology Evaluation Methods”. However, due to the fact that this guideline focuses on methodological assessment and lacks detailed research report standards, methodological suggestions, and validation methods, it cannot effectively guide the reporting of network pharmacology research. Therefore, many reports on network pharmacology still rely on STROBE statements, CONSORT statements, and the 2017 CONSORT-CHM format statements as references for research design and reporting. However, these lists are mainly designed for reporting observational studies or clinical randomized controlled trials, and thus are not applicable to the analysis of traditional Chinese medicine network pharmacology. This has hindered the high-quality development of traditional Chinese medicine. This study referred to the relevant content of the “Guidelines for Network Pharmacology Evaluation Methods”, reviewed relevant literature in domestic and foreign databases, and combined with traditional Chinese medicine theory and the core concept of “syndrome”, summarized and integrated the key points of reporting in traditional Chinese medicine network pharmacology, thereby promoting high-quality reporting in this field.

title: META-TTE - Transparent reporting of meta-analyses of time-to-event outcomes based on aggregate data from randomised trials of interventions
text:
Poor reporting of time-to-event analyses in trial publications, including outcome definitions, general and time-to-event specific methods and study characteristics can hinder the development of time-to-event meta-analyses.
To address these limitations and to improve the reporting of such meta-analyses, a group from Germany is developing a reporting guideline to be used em conjunction with PRISMA, but specifically focused on time-to-event outcomes.
The group is conducting an online open survey among experts in evidence synthesis, methodologists and statisticians to identify and confirm relevant reporting items and their definition. After a first round of feedback, they will invite participants for consultatory calls, to discuss discrepancies.
The group has-registered a protocol at OSF: https://osf.io/j5bmw. They plan to publish the reporting guidelines in late 2024, as open-access documents if funding becomes available for that.

title: Orthopaedic CAse REport Reporting Guideline
text:
Orthopaedic case reports constitute an important source of early clinical insight, highlighting rare presentations, novel surgical approaches, implant-related complications, and unexpected outcomes across trauma, arthroplasty, spine, sports medicine, paediatric orthopaedics, and oncology. Despite their widespread use, the reporting quality of orthopaedic case reports remains highly variable. Current general case-reporting frameworks—most notably the CARE guideline and the surgery-focused SCARE guideline—have significantly improved transparency in their respective domains, but they do not fully address orthopaedic-specific requirements such as implant specifications, fixation strategies, biomechanical considerations, classification systems, rehabilitation protocols, imaging standards, or functional outcome measures.
Orthopaedic case reports frequently include device-related details and operative nuances that demand greater specificity than what current generic reporting tools provide. As a result, essential information is often missing or inconsistently reported, limiting educational value, hindering reproducibility, and reducing the usefulness of these reports for clinicians, trainees, and researchers.
O-CARE aims to address this gap by developing a dedicated, consensus-based reporting guideline tailored specifically to orthopaedic case reports. This guideline will:

Provide a structured checklist covering all key domains of orthopaedic case reporting.
Enhance the completeness, clarity, and clinical relevance of case reports across all orthopaedic subspecialties. Support authors, reviewers, and journal editors in evaluating and improving case report quality.
Facilitate future systematic synthesis of case-based evidence and improve the reporting of early signals related to new implants, techniques, and complications.

O-CARE will be developed via a rigorous multi-phase process, involving a Steering Committee of experts in orthopaedics and reporting methodology, and a broad Delphi panel including surgeons, methodologists, journal editors, and allied specialists. The final guideline will be applicable internationally and will be offered as an open-access resource to maximize uptake and impact.
