title: Reporting Guidelines for Organoid-Based Clinical Trials: An Extension of the CONSORT Statement
text:
Organoids are stem cell- or tissue-derived three-dimensional structures that recapitulate the key pathological features and genetic background of their tissue of origin. They offer a physiologically relevant model for simulating human organ development, function, and disease progression, while overcoming limitations inherent to animal models, such as species-specific differences in metabolism and immune responses. Their spatial architecture and cellular fidelity enable real-time observation of disease dynamics, and when combined with gene-editing technologies, organoids facilitate rapid validation of gene functions or therapeutic targets, significantly enhancing experimental reproducibility. Moreover, organoid models align with the “3Rs” principle—Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement—by reducing the reliance on animal models for drug toxicity testing and lowering associated research and development costs. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and pharmaceutical research institutions recommend organoid research as an effective alternative to animal experiments.
The increasing number of organoid-related clinical trials in recent years further underscores the need of establishing clinical guidelines. As interest in organoid research continues to grow, so does the need for standardized reporting guidelines. However, no dedicated reporting framework currently exists for organoid-based clinical trials, increasing the risk of incomplete reporting and the prevalence of spin. For example, clinical trials involving organoids typically require reporting on the organoid’s composition, source, and the gene editing techniques used. But, the CONSORT guidelines do not include items addressing this information.
Therefore, the project leads advocate for the development of a reporting guideline specific to organoid clinical trials. Such a guideline would not only improve the quality and transparency of organoid research reporting but also facilitate the translation of basic science into clinical applications, ultimately accelerating the advancement of personalized medicine and interdisciplinary innovation.

title: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses - PRISMA Extension of Preclinical In Vivo Animal Experiments
text:
This reporting guideline is an extension to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA), specifically for systematic reviews research performed in preclinical, in vivo animal models. The guideline development will occur in five phases: 1) Group establishment to help and provide expertise in the guideline development; 2) A cross-sectional study to describe the characteristics of and assess the reporting of contemporary preclinical systematic reviews; 3) Delphi Exercise; 4) Written Guidance, and 5) Dissemination. The Core Group (n=14 to date) will lead the development and dissemination of the guidelines and includes members with expertise in various disciplines pertinent to guideline development, systematic reviews and meta-analysis, and in vivo animal experiments. This group formed in Fall 2018 and finalized its membership in February 2020. The group have performed an environmental scan by systematically searching the literature for published preclinical systematic reviews and have identified and synthesized the characteristics of these reviews in Summer 2019. The Delphi will start in Summer 2020 and finish in Fall 2020. The group aims to finalize the guidelines and have the results of the environmental scan and conference proceedings submitted for publication by Winter 2021.
The protocol for the overall project has been publicly posted on Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/g4kqz/. Within this project, the protocols for the cross-sectional study and the Delphi study have been posted as project components.

title: PROM-GRIP - Patient-Reported Outcome Measures - Guideline for Reporting In clinical Practice
text:
Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are aspects of a patient’s health status that are reported directly by the patient, without interpretation by a healthcare provider or anyone else, which are measured using Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs). According to the developers of this reporting guideline, there is no consensus on what constitutes complete and sufficient reporting in studies of PROM use in clinical practice. Factors such as healthcare provider training in PROM use, how PROM scores are fed back, whether instructions are given on how to act on PROM scores, and whether the patient receives feedback on PROM scores are potentially important points to report. However, there is currently a great deal of variability in what studies report about the use of PROMs in clinical practice. The goal of the group is to improve the quality of reporting in studies that illustrate or evaluate the use of PROMs in clinical practice.
The guideline will be applicable to any study design in which PROMS are used. Development started in 2023, with a systematic review, and a two-round Delphi survey and a consensus meeting are planned, as well as piloting. An implementation and integrated knowledge translation plan will follow. The project is being developed without funding so far, but the group plans to publish the reporting guideline as an open access document in 2025.

title: HOTTER: Heat therapy: Optimising Transparency Through Essential Reporting
text:
The HOTTER (Heat therapy: Optimising Transparency Through Essential Reporting) statement will establish minimum reporting requirements for human research investigating the physiological and health effects of heat therapy. It will cover whole-body and local heating modalities (e.g. footbaths, water perfused pants), including sauna bathing, hot-water immersion, infrared heating, and other externally applied heating interventions, used independently or alongside treatments such as exercise.

The guideline will address reporting across experimental and observational study designs, encompassing acute exposures and repeated interventions in healthy and clinical populations. Proposed reporting domains include participant characteristics and prior heat exposure; heating modality and equipment; environmental conditions; exposure frequency, intensity, duration, and progression; physiological responses and thermal dose assessment; co-interventions; adherence; and adverse events. Requirements will distinguish prescribed exposure from exposure actually received and identify how relevant parameters were measured.

Developed through international multidisciplinary consensus, HOTTER will complement established reporting guidelines, including CONSORT, STROBE, and TIDieR. Its purpose is to improve transparency, reproducibility, interpretation, and evidence synthesis, rather than prescribe optimal treatment protocols or establish clinical efficacy. Oncological hyperthermia, thermal ablation, and research focused exclusively on occupational or environmental heat stress will fall outside its scope.

title: STROBE-D: Strengthening the Reporting og Observational Studies in Epidemiology for Drowning (STROBE-D): An extension of the STROBE statement for drowning research
text:
Drowning remains a significant global health issue, yet much of the research in this field is observational in nature due to ethical, practical, and logistical constraints. Despite the availability of the STROBE statement, adherence to these guidelines within the drowning research community has been inconsistent and often incomplete. A preliminary analysis from our ongoing systematic review indicates that fewer than 50% of published observational drowning studies fully comply with the original STROBE checklist.
This lack of adherence suggests that the current STROBE framework may not sufficiently capture the unique aspects of drowning-related research, which often includes highly context-specific variables such as environmental conditions, rescue logistics, water safety practices, resuscitation details, and outcome classification based on diverse international definitions. As a result, many key methodological elements and contextual factors are either underreported or inconsistently presented, hindering reproducibility, critical appraisal, and evidence synthesis.
To address these limitations, we propose the development of a STROBE extension specifically tailored to drowning-related observational studies. The goal is not to replace the core STROBE framework but to build upon it by incorporating drowning-specific reporting elements that improve clarity, transparency, and comparability across studies. Such an extension would provide structured guidance for authors, reviewers, and editors, helping to standardise reporting practices.

title: BRIDGE-AI reporting guideline for cross-design evaluation studies of artificial intelligence in digital health diagnosis, clinical decision support, and post-deployment monitoring.
text:
BRIDGE stands for Bias Reduction for Implementation, Deployment, Governance, and Equity. BRIDGE-AI is a new, cross-design reporting guideline for evaluation studies of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital health, particularly diagnosis, prognosis, clinical decision support, workflow integration, and post-deployment monitoring. It is not conceived as an extension of a single existing guideline. Instead, it addresses reporting items that cut across study designs and evaluation phases and are currently dispersed across the AI literature.
The guideline is organised around eight workgroups: WG1 fairness and data representativeness; WG2 robustness and stress-testing; WG3 traceability, documentation and accountability; WG4 explainability and transparency; WG5 usability, human-AI interaction and automation bias; WG6 governance, ethical oversight and regulatory alignment; WG7 clinical and public health integration/workflow evaluation; and WG8 post-deployment monitoring, drift detection and lifecycle quality.
Candidate reporting items are also being grounded in ISO/IEC standards and technical specifications, including ISO/IEC TR 24027 and ISO/IEC TS 12791 for bias and unwanted bias treatment, ISO/IEC TR 24028 for trustworthiness and transparency, ISO/IEC TR 24029-1 and ISO/IEC 24029-2 for robustness assessment, ISO/IEC 23894 for AI risk management, and ISO/IEC TS 4213 for machine learning classification performance assessment.
A new guideline is needed because existing AI guidance on EQUATOR is largely design-specific or phase-specific—for example trials, protocols, diagnostic accuracy studies, prediction models, or early-stage clinical evaluation—whereas trustworthy digital health evaluation also requires consistent reporting of subgroup performance, oversight, lifecycle monitoring, workflow fit, and post-deployment drift. BRIDGE-AI will therefore complement existing guidance while remaining a standalone new reporting guideline entry.

title: PRISMA-probiotics: Extension for probiotics
text:
Systematic reviews are essential tools for synthesizing evidence and informing clinical decision-making. The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) statement provides a standardized framework to enhance the transparency and completeness of reporting in systematic reviews. However, specific domains—such as the use of probiotics in clinical and experimental research—present unique challenges that are not fully addressed by the core PRISMA checklist.
Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits to the host. Their use spans various disciplines including gastroenterology, immunology, pediatrics, gerontology, and psychiatry - amongst others-, and the body of evidence surrounding their efficacy and safety continues to grow. Nevertheless, systematic reviews in this field often suffer from poor reporting related to key probiotic-specific variables, such as strain identification, dosage, viability, delivery format, duration of administration, and host factors influencing outcomes. These omissions limit the reproducibility of findings, reduce the utility of reviews for clinicians and policymakers, and hinder the translation of research into practice.
This PRISMA extension aims to fill this gap by providing a specialized reporting guideline tailored to systematic reviews involving probiotics. It will build upon the core PRISMA 2020 framework, while adding targeted items that reflect the complexity and specificity of probiotic interventions. The extension will help ensure that systematic reviews in this field report essential details that enable proper interpretation, replication, and application of findings. There is a pressing need for this extension due to the increasing number of published reviews on probiotics, many of which vary greatly in quality and reporting standards. By improving consistency and transparency, the PRISMA-Probiotics extension will enhance the value of systematic reviews for all stakeholders—including researchers, clinicians, guideline developers, and patients—and ultimately support better evidence-based decisions in the use of probiotics.

title: LIGHTS–LAMPES: a two-level reporting guideline for clinical, laboratory and pre-clinical studies of therapeutic light-based and laser interventions in photomedicine
text:
LIGHTS–LAMPES is a reporting guideline under development for studies delivering optical radiation as a therapeutic or interventional agent. Its scope covers photobiomodulation and low-level laser therapy, light-emitting diode phototherapy, intense pulsed light, therapeutic ultraviolet phototherapy, illumination for photodynamic therapy, and surgical or high-power laser interventions. It is intended for clinical trials, experimental laboratory and pre-clinical investigations, and study protocols where optical exposure must be reproducibly described.
The guideline addresses gaps in the reproducibility of optical dosimetry. The eight minimum reporting parameters of Jenkins and Carroll (2011) were developed primarily for laser photomedicine, whereas the ENLIGHT checklist is directed at ocular non-visual responses to light. Taken together, these instruments do not provide a single cross-source framework for characterising tissue-directed therapeutic exposures across both laser and non-laser systems. Inconsistent description of irradiance, radiant exposure, illuminated area at the target, emission timing and calibration complicates comparison and replication.
The proposed two-level structure comprises LIGHTS, with six core domains relevant to any therapeutic light source (source and wavelength; irradiance and power; geometry and beam area; temporal pattern; duration and treatment schedule; target site and safety), and LAMPES, with six supplementary domains for laser systems (lasing medium; delivery architecture; emission mode; peak-power profile; beam quality; and safety classification). The framework is designed to complement general intervention-reporting tools such as TIDieR rather than replace them, while focusing on metrological traceability and clearly specified quantities at the exposed target.

title: QRDC-RG - Qualitative Remote Data Collection Reporting Guideline
text:
Remote methods of qualitative data collection are those characterised by physical distance between the researcher/s and participant/s, use of technology to communicate and where there is an in-person equivalent method. Whilst use of remote qualitative data collection methods has proliferated in recent years, there are currently no guidelines for reporting these studies. Existing reporting guidelines for qualitative research (e.g. COREQ, SRQR) do not include items on technologically mediated study designs, only technologies used to record data (e.g. dictaphones). While developing guidance for qualitative remote data collection, the research team noted that reporting of remotely conducted qualitative research studies is inconsistent and often lacks key details of the research design that can significantly impact data quality. These include choice of technology, visibility of researcher, what ‘counts’ as data (e.g. comments in chat/emojis) and the synchronicity of the data collection.
The QRDC reporting guideline (QRDC-RG) will focus on the reporting of data collection methods - from sampling through to data processing for analysis. It will complement existing guidelines for reporting qualitative research by focusing on research design decisions that are unique to remotely conducted and hybrid (remote and in-person methods combined) research. It will be broadly applicable across a range of qualitative data collection methods where there is an in-person equivalent (e.g. interviews, focus groups, observation). The research team plan to conduct a review of existing guidelines and evidence on the quality of remote research reporting. A diverse international group of researchers and stakeholders will be appointed and a Delphi exercise and consensus meeting will be held to develop the checklist items. The team aim to work with qualitative health journals to secure endorsement and to support the adherence of authors and reviewers. Training and a launch webinar will be developed and the guideline will be translated into several languages to support international uptake.

title: RIGHT 2.0: Reporting Items for practice Guidelines in HealThcare
text:
More than nine years have passed since the publication of the first version of the RIGHT checklist (https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/right-statement/). Recently, factors such as user feedback from guideline interest-holders (including guideline developers, journal peer reviewers and editors, guideline users, guideline researchers, and policymakers), continuous innovations and developments in the field of guideline methodology (e.g., living guidelines and rapid recommendations), and the global surge of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have further accelerated the need to update the RIGHT. Taking AI technology as an example, large language models can play a key auxiliary role in guideline development, e.g. by assisting in the formulation of clinical questions and accelerating different steps of evidence synthesis like the development of search strategies, literature screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. However, there are currently no specific recommendations on how to standardize the reporting of related processes. The rapid evolvement in methodologies has also given motivation to updates of other reporting and evaluation tools. Based on these considerations, the RIGHT Working Group has initiated the update process of the checklist with the aim of providing a more applicable guideline reporting standard.

title: The reporting for Chinese herbal medicine placebo guidelines in randomized controlled trials
text:
As a crucial component in verifying the efficacy of medications, placebos play an important role in randomized controlled trials of Chinese herbal medicine (CHM). The CONSORT Extension for Chinese Herbal Medicine Formulas 2017: Recommendations, Explanation, and Elaboration, includes five items specifically addressing the reporting of CHM-placebo. However, an epidemiological evaluation conducted by our team on randomized controlled trials of CHM containing CHM-placebo published between January 2018 and September 2025 revealed that compliance with these items was generally low. In particular, there were serious omissions regarding “Name and amount of each ingredient”, “Description of the similarity of placebo with the intervention”, “Quality control and safety assessment, if any”, “Production information: where, when, how, and by whom the placebo was produced”. Some studies merely mentioned the CHM-placebo had a similar appearance to CHM without specifying their exact composition, preparation process, or degree of similarity to the test drug in terms of physical properties. Most studies did not report the results of placebo quality control tests, nor did they clarify whether the CHM-placebo’s safety had been verified prior to the trial. These missing details directly impacted the trial’s safety assessment, transparency, and success rate of blinding.
Compared to fields such as acupuncture and surgery, reporting guidelines for CHM-placebo still have significant room for improvement. For acupuncture, two specific reporting standards—ACURATE and SHARE—have been established. The former specifies reporting requirements from the perspective of operational procedures, while the latter emphasizes the reporting of acupuncture details such as patient positioning, needle insertion angle, and needle equipment information, as well as non-therapeutic contextual factors such as doctor-patient communication and practitioner qualifications. In the field of surgery, the ASPIRE guidelines systematically outline the design principles for sham surgery, including identifying key elements by deconstructing surgical procedures, defining levels of placebo fidelity, and implementing risk-minimization strategies. These guidelines are grounded in the complexity of interventions within their respective fields and emphasize comprehensive reporting throughout the entire process, from design to implementation. In contrast, the production process of CHM-placebos involves multiple stages, including excipient selection, and sensory simulation such as appearance, odor, and taste, making it complex. However, there is currently a lack of targeted, comprehensive reporting standards for CHM-placebo.
This guideline will draw on experience from the aforementioned fields and, based on existing issues, specify the items to be reported and set out specific requirements, covering the entire process of CHM-placebo from production to usage. This guideline aims to enhance the safety, transparency, and blinding success rate of randomized controlled trials of CHM, thereby ensuring the reliability and reproducibility of the trial results. This guideline is intended for researchers, journal editors, and peer reviewers involved in conducting, reviewing, or publishing such studies.

title: Standards of reporting for studies on medical grade footwear for adults
text:
Medical grade footwear is frequently prescribed in the treatment and prevention of many different diseases, with the aim of increasing people’s capacity for mobility. This footwear, which is a combination of the shoes and its insole, can achieve improved mobility in many different ways, such as by enhancing stability, supporting deformities, reducing pain, protecting from trauma or redistributing plantar pressure. As medical grade footwear is also a device with many different components, entangling the beneficial, the non-effective and the potentially harmful effects of (components of) such footwear is complex, and requires careful and high-quality scientific studies.
Studies on medical grade footwear are ever more frequent. A quick search on PubMed on 10 October 2025 shows that at this moment 25% of all >15,000 publications in this field are from the last 5 years, while 55% of all >380 systematic reviews have been published after 2020. While these studies have generated important insights in the effectiveness of medical grade footwear, a consistent theme in the systematic reviews done is the lack of high-quality studies. Initiatives to improve scientific quality of studies on medical grade footwear are needed.
In various systematic reviews on medical grade footwear, it was concluded that study reporting could be improved. Large variations were especially seen in the descriptions of the footwear that investigated, while complete, clear and consistent reporting is required. This hampers risk of bias assessment of these studies, and limits the opportunities to adequately inform clinical decision-making. This has led to calls for the development of standards of reporting for studies on medical grade footwear interventions.
We have searched the EQUATOR-network, pubmed and grey literature, and currently no reporting standards for studies on medical grade footwear are available or under development. With millions of adult patients relying on medical grade footwear, with thousands of yearly publications, and with consistent calls for higher quality reporting of this complex medical device, our aim is to develop standards of reporting for studies on medical grade footwear.

title: PRISTINE: Preferred Reporting Items for Syntheses Through Interactive, Navigable Evidence-portals
text:
The promise of large language models to not only screen and extract data from studies (Gartlehner et al., 2024) but also summarise them (Ovelman et al., 2024) makes one-stop shop websites for answering decision-makers’ questions closer than ever before, yet no formal guidance exists for creators of such websites.
Evidence portals are websites that provide reliable web-based summaries of research findings, offering accessible insights without the need to consult individual studies (Gough and White, 2018). If successful, they can serve as a go-to knowledge platform for policymakers and other decision-makers, including frontline professionals (nurses, teachers, etc), seeking clarity on what is likely to work, when, how, for whom and at what cost. A prominent example is the Teaching and Learning Toolkit developed by the Education Endowment Foundation, with most school leaders in England who report using it to make decisions (Higgins et al., 2022).
Due to the intensive nature of knowledge translation required (e.g. the necessity to create meticulous evidence standards that underpin them), few of them exist at scale and are kept up to date, but that will soon change. Recently, significant resources were committed to the development of infrastructure to create living evidence synthesis (Behavioural Insights Team, 2024; Wellcome Trust, 2024). To increase evidence synthesis findings uptake for busy policymakers and practitioners, the recently formed Evidence Synthesis Infrastructure Collaborative recommends that information previously contained in text-based PDF reports be reported using interactive, web-based interfaces. While guidance for visual and interactive maps is already in progress (PRISMA-Evidence Gap Map extension), no formal guidance exists for evidence portals. I coordinated the web development for the International Initiative for Impact Evaluation’s Development Evidence Portal. Based on that experience, I believe this emerging field would benefit from building on the work of Gough and White (2018), who provided early recommendations for portal creators based on an analysis of 14 English-language portals. Their recommendations are limited to evidence of effectiveness. Using the theoretical framework of research uptake developed by Higgins et al (2022) their focus seems to be on accuracy (internal and external validity) and to a lesser degree also applicability and actionability. They do not provide much guidance on the remaining dimensions of research use that may be sacrificed with too much focus on accuracy. These competing dimensions that I suggest focusing on are accessibility, appropriateness and acceptability. These dimensions would be explored using the following research questions:

How to make portals reporting relevant for a broader range of study designs?
Which information is key to present in the portal’s web-based elements, how to make it easily accessible?
How to report equity considerations and involvement of stakeholders (particularly patients and the public)?
How to use web-based, interactive features to increase the portal’s usefulness, actionability and to whom?

title: Survey Aware Machine Learning (SaML) Statement: Reporting Items for Machine Learning Studies Using Complex Sample Survey Data
text:
Machine learning (ML) is increasingly applied to different large-scale surveys, such as national health surveys like NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey), BRFSS (Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System), and NHIS (National Health Interview Survey). Often, such surveys use complex sampling designs with stratification, clustering by primary sampling units, and unequal selection probabilities handled through sampling weights. Standard ML assumes i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) data and ignores these design features. These survey design features are relevant at multiple stages of the pipeline, including data splitting, model training, performance evaluation, and uncertainty quantification. Without survey aware machine learning (SaML), results may risk biased population estimates, underestimated uncertainty, and unreliable fairness assessments. It is imperative that appropriate considerations be made when using such surveys with ML-based methods.
Existing reporting guidelines address related areas but are incomplete for robust SaML. Preferred Reporting Items for Complex Sample Survey Analysis (PRICSSA) (Seidenberg et al., 2023) standardizes reporting for complex survey analysis, including design, weighting, and variance estimation, but does not cover ML pipelines. TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis)+AI (Collins et al., 2024) standardizes reporting for ML-based prediction models but does not address survey design features such as weights or clustering. As survey design interacts with ML workflows at every stage, this gap cannot be address by extending either guideline independently.
The SaML statement targets this gap. It specifies what information should be reported when applying ML modelling to complex survey data, including choices regarding data splitting, model training, tuning, evaluation, uncertainty and calibration. An initial scoping review of methodological studies (in progress) shows that prior work addresses individual steps but does not provide integrated reporting guidance. Key gaps include whether data splitting respects cluster structure, how sampling weights enter the loss, whether tuning uses design-adjusted metrics, and whether performance reflects the target population.
The need for holistic reporting guidelines for SaML is clear. Recent analyses report that NHANES-based publications nearly doubled from 4926 in 2023, to 7876 in 2024, with many studies applying ML methods without accounting for the complex survey design (Suchak et al., 2025). The SaML statement defines a minimum reporting guidelines that complements PRICSSA and TRIPOD+AI and ensures the ML studies using survey data report the information needed for transparent, reproducible, and population-valid inference.

title: AD ASTRA – SPIRIT and CONSORT extensions for dog-assisted interventions
text:

Most existing DAI evidence is based on small studies with scientific flaws, which lack important details when published, including the risks to both human and dog partners.
The AD ASTRA group will develop SPIRIT and CONSORT extensions for trials involving DAIs. The statements will provide authors with a standard reporting structure to facilitate completeness and transparency and aid in critical appraisal and interpretation of DAIs.
Representatives will be invited from dog-assisted intervention providers, clinicians, academics, and patients/their caregiver/support teams, to participate in the development. A systematic review will be conducted to identify randomised controlled trials using DAIs and reporting gaps. A Delphi survey and consensus workshop will finalise the items. title: GRACE - Guidelines for the Reporting of A Clinical Electroencephalogram (EEG) in the medical literature
text:
The results of clinical electroencephalograms (EEGs) are frequently described in case reports and other types of studies in the scientific literature. These can add crucial diagnostic and prognostic information. However, the way in which such reports is described is very variable.

title: GRRAS-COSMIN: Guidelines for Reporting Reliability and Agreement Studies-Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments
text:
The current version of the Guidelines for Reporting Reliability and Agreement Studies (GRRAS) were published in 2011. Although the GRRAS are still widely applied, they are outdated compared to methodological developments regarding health research reporting guidelines in recent years. Substantial advances have been made regarding sample size determination and other aspects in reliability and agreement studies. In addition, the development of the current GRRAS did not follow the state-of-the-art guidance for developers of health research reporting guidelines, because that were not yet available at the time of GRRAS development. Therefore, an update of the GRRAS according to the current standards of reporting guideline development is needed.Additionally, this update aims to harmonize and align wordings and concepts with relavant related initiatives such as the COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN), to improve usability and uptake of the-updated guidelines. Recently, COSMIN developed a tool to assess the risk of bias of reliability and agreement/measurement error studies and of systematic reviews of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures. Similarly, Lucas et al. published a quality appraisal tool for studies of diagnostic reliability (QAREL), which also applies to reliability and agreement studies. Although study reporting and risk of bias assessments are fundamentally different, both approaches should be harmonized. Only what is reported can be assessed. Therefore, reporting guidelines must contain the items for which the risk of bias is assessed.

title: RepOrting standards for Systematic Evidence Syntheses (ROSES): an update to reporting standards for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and systematic maps in environmental sciences
text:
The ROSES Update revises the RepOrting standards for Systematic Evidence Syntheses (ROSES), originally developed to support transparent reporting of systematic reviews and systematic maps in environmental management. The updated guideline is intended for authors, peer reviewers, editors, and other users of environmental evidence syntheses, with development focused first on systematic reviews (including meta-analyses) and subsequently extended to systematic maps. Since ROSES was first published in 2017, reporting expectations and evidence-synthesis practice have shifted considerably as automation tools are increasingly applied across key stages of the review process. The development team has also identified persistent gaps in reporting completeness within environmental evidence syntheses, gaps that reduce transparency, hinder replication and reuse, and make it difficult to determine precisely what was done in a given review. The updated guideline will draw on existing ROSES materials, a new item bank compiled from evidence-synthesis reporting guidelines and standards across multiple disciplines and review types, structured consensus processes involving methodological experts, broader stakeholder survey feedback, and validation exercises assessing usability and repeatability. Planned outputs include updated ROSES forms and flow diagrams, supporting development documentation, and an explanation-and-elaboration document, together aimed at promoting more complete, transparent, and consistent reporting of environmental evidence syntheses. title: Research reporting guidelines for health RESearch involving People who arE inCarceraTed: The RESPECT Guidelines
text:
The scope of this guideline is: Original research that involves people experiencing incarceration or detention in a correctional facility as participants and that includes a focus on health. The guidelines will apply to all methodologies. We define correctional facility as designated facilities that hold people remanded to custody or following sentencing related to the criminal legal system including jails, prison, penitentiaries, etc. We define health as per the World Health Organization: a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This includes studies of healthcare.
People who experience incarceration experience substantial health inequities. Research represents an important strategy to improve population health, but there are unique considerations and challenges inherent in conducting research involving people who are incarcerated. Research involving people in custody is often reported badly and missing information needed for appropriate interpretation and use such as project covernance (e.g. role of correctional authority), ethical issues (e.g. how participants were recruited) and sampling (e.g. whether purposive, or whole population). Research reporting guidelines are a proven strategy to strengthen research reporting, and may positively influence research standards and practices. Additionally, though less common than guidelines for methodologies or conditions, guidelines for research involving specific populations (such as the CONSIDER statement for strengthening reporting of health research involving Indigenous Peoples) are an important resource for addressing inequities in health and health research. However, there are currently no research reporting guidelines for research involving people who are incarcerated as participants.

title: The Systematic Engine: A Diagnostic Reporting Guideline for Critical Appraisal Processes in Evidence Synthesis
text:
This guideline addresses the critical gap in transparent reporting of the process and implementation of critical appraisal within systematic reviews and meta-analyses. While tools like PRISMA guide the reporting of the review itself, and tools like Cochrane RoB 2 guide the assessment, there is no standardized framework for reporting how these assessments are performed, integrated, and used to transform the evidence. The Systematic Engine reframes critical appraisal from a procedural checkpoint to the central, diagnostic engine of synthesis. A new reporting guideline is needed because:
Current reporting of appraisal is often opaque, with judgments and rationales inadequately documented, hindering reproducibility.
The linkage between domain-based bias assessments (e.g., from RoB 2, ROBINS-I) and downstream methodological decisions (sensitivity analyses, GRADE certainty ratings, narrative conclusions) is frequently unclear or unreported.
There is high subjectivity and inconsistency in how appraisal tools are applied, with insufficient reporting of team calibration and disagreement resolution processes.
This guideline will provide a structured checklist for reporting the four core functions of the Systematic Engine model: (1) deconstruction and profiling; (2) stratification and weighting; (3) certainty calibration; and 4 interpretive guarding.

title: Checklist for Reporting Valuation Studies of Multi-Attribute Utility-Based Instruments – Collaborative Involvement
text:
Collaboration with parties beyond the core research team is increasingly recognised as important. Potential ‘collaborators’ can include individuals, organisations or communities beyond the core research team that have a direct interest in the process and outcomes of a project, research or policy endeavour. By extension, we define ‘collaborative involvement’ (CI) in research as an activity/activities between the core research team and collaborators that are conducted on a peer-to-peer level that is designed to help inform, interpret, implement, disseminate, and/or evaluate research. Collaborators have a right to be involved in research that affects them. CI activities help ensure that the needs of collaborators are at the core of research activities and in turn can help improve the value of research, such as by increasing its relevance to patients, supporting recruitment, and enhancing dissemination. Many health research funding bodies now require and promote the engagement of collaborators.
While CI now forms a core part of many aspects of health and care research, it appears to be less consistent within health state valuation research specifically (i.e., research that aims to derive people’s quantitative preferences for living in different health states). Largely, CI in health state valuation appears to have been limited to helping to inform health state descriptions for use in valuation studies, yet there are multiple instances where CI could be incorporated, such as supporting diverse recruitment and helping explain valuation methods to participants. CI in health state valuation contrasts that within related disciplines, such as patient-reported outcome measure development where recommendations for incorporating CI already exist.
Facilitating consistent, high-quality CI in health state valuation is thus a necessary step to ‘future-proof’ the discipline. Integral to this will be the development of a set of best practice guidelines and reporting checklist to help promote quality and transparency as CI within health state valuation research develops. In previous work, a scoping review was conducted to identify emerging recommendations for best practice in CI in health state valuation and a 15-item framework was synthesised. The current project aims to build on this initial research and develop a set of robust, agreed-upon best practice guidelines for CI in health state valuation, and an extension to the Checklist for Reporting Valuation Studies of Multi-Attribute Utility-Based Instruments (CREATE) (CREATE-CI).

title: A reporting guideline for research into outcomes following release from correctional and forensic settings
text:
The scope of this guideline is to provide recommendations for studies reporting key health and justice outcomes for discharged forensic patients and people released from prison settings returning to the community. Specifically, the guideline aims to provide recommendations for standardising the way in which post discharge and release community outcomes, including reoffending, readmissions and mortality, are defined, measured, recorded, analysed, and reported. A standardised approach will improve comparability between studies, settings, and samples, allowing future meta-analytic syntheses.
In undertaking a systematic systematic review and meta-analysis of post-discharge outcomes for forensic mental health patients, it was evident that published studies varied enormously in approaches to outcome reporting. In particular, the following problems were identified:

Most studies provide sufficient demographic details for the main sample, but often fail to report the same details consistently when reporting on the sub-samples that might be different from the main cohort (e.g., patients who remained in hospital vs those who were eventually discharged into the community)
Reoffending outcomes are often inconsistently defined, with some studies using reoffending and reconvictions interchangeably, for example.
Outcomes are sometimes not defined in studies. For example, some authors may provide details on what is counted as “violent offending”, while others do not explicitly define it.
There is sometimes insufficient data transparency regarding the sample/cohort. Information about the location of secure hospitals, catchment areas, and whether the sample is drawn from a previously established dataset is often lacking. Follow-up durations are inconsistently reported. This makes it difficult to calculate person-years at-risk and prohibits comparisons being made between cohorts.
Post-release reoffending outcomes for people being released from prison settings are reported without the information required to calculate person-years at risk, which further prevents comparison. These outcomes tend to be reported as cumulative prevalence rates (with varying durations of observation) only.

title: SPoRTIER: Social Prescribing Reporting Template to Improve Evaluation and Replication

SPoRTIER will provide a standardised useable template to capture contextual details on different programmes and how these programmes are being implemented to aid understanding of how social prescribing contributes to changes in health and wellbeing. title: The CSS-EIC Statement: Consensus on Research Ethics and Integrity in Sports Science (Chinese Expert Consensus)
text:
Background: Sports science research in China has experienced exponential growth in recent years. However, the development of specific ethical norms has lagged behind this quantitative expansion. General guidelines (e.g., Declaration of Helsinki) do not fully address the unique challenges inherent to sports science, particularly within the context of high-performance sport.
Scope & Aim: This project aims to develop the “China Sports Science Ethics & Integrity Checklist (CSS-EIC).” It is a consensus-based reporting guideline designed to bridge the gap between international ethical standards and specific local research practices.
Key Issues Addressed: The guideline covers six key domains:
Participant Rights: Addressing power dynamics in athlete recruitment (e.g., coach-athlete relationships) and ensuring non-coercion.
Safety & Anti-Doping: Establishing physiological cut-off criteria for maximal exertion tests and ensuring strict WADA compliance for supplement studies.
Methodological Rigor: Promoting transparency in intervention reporting (based on TIDieR/CERF) and scientific justification for invasive procedures. Data Privacy: Managing data ownership disputes (team vs. researcher) and de-identification of high-profile elite athletes.
Animal Welfare: Specific ethics for forced exercise models. Research Integrity: Addressing authorship disputes and data management.

title: PRITERS - Preferred Reporting Items for Replication of Systematic Reviews
text:
Systematic reviews are considered the gold standard for synthesizing evidence to inform research, practice, and policy. However, the reliability and validity of systematic review findings could depend heavily on their reproducibility and replicability. Replication of systematic reviews would play a critical role in verifying results, identifying potential biases, and updating evidence to reflect new data. Despite its importance, the reporting of systematic review replication studies is rare. As an emerging field the adoption of guidelines will support consistency, transparency, and rigor.
Existing reporting guidelines, such as PRISMA, provide comprehensive frameworks for conducting and reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses but do not address the unique challenges and requirements of replication studies. These include documenting variations in replication methodologies, specifying the rationale for replication, and reporting discrepancies between original and replicated findings.
The Preferred Reporting Items for Replication of Systematic Reviews: PRITERS Statement aims to fill this gap by providing a standardized reporting framework tailored to replication studies in systematic reviews. It is designed to enhance transparency, reproducibility, and comparability across replication studies while promoting the integrity of evidence synthesis. PRITERS will guide researchers in clearly reporting:
1. The justification, purpose and scope of the replication (e.g., direct replication, conceptual replication, or methodological critique). 2. Any modifications or updates made to the original systematic review protocol (including those made during conduct of the review). 3. Detailed comparisons of methods, results, and conclusions between the original and replicated reviews. 4. Limitations and implications of the replication findings.
By ensuring clarity and uniformity in reporting, PRITERS will support researchers, journal editors, and policy-makers in evaluating the robustness of systematic review findings and in identifying areas for methodological improvement. Ultimately, PRITERS aims to strengthen the credibility and reliability of systematic reviews as foundational tools for evidence-based decision-making.

title: ReRT-REPORT: A cross-design reporting guideline for reirradiation studies
text:
Reirradiation (reRT) is increasingly used across tumor sites, supported by advances in imaging, treatment planning, and delivery that enable safer retreatment strategies. However, reRT studies remain highly heterogeneous in their reporting, particularly regarding prior irradiation, cumulative dose evaluation, assumptions on tissue recovery, target definition, organ-at-risk constraints, and the integration of prior and current treatment courses. While this heterogeneity reflects clinical complexity, inconsistencies in how these elements are reported severely limit comparability between studies, weaken evidence synthesis, and hinder the development of robust and transferable clinical knowledge.
Existing reporting guidelines from the EQUATOR Network, including CONSORT, STROBE, and TRIPOD, have substantially improved research transparency but do not address the specific methodological challenges inherent to reRT, such as the integration of multi-course radiotherapy data and cumulative dose assessment. Building upon recent consensus efforts that established standards for dose evaluation and clinical workflows, recent ESTRO-endorsed initiatives have further highlighted major inconsistencies in terminology, reporting practices, and dose evaluation methods, reinforcing the need for structured and standardized reporting.
This project aims to develop a dedicated cross-design reporting guideline for reRT studies, aligned with existing EQUATOR frameworks while addressing the specific complexities of reirradiation. The guideline will define a minimal set of mandatory reporting items, applicable across study designs, tumour sites, and radiotherapy techniques.
The primary objective is to develop a structured reporting guideline to improve reproducibility, comparability, and clinical interpretability of reRT research. As a secondary implementation tool, a structured eCRF-like framework may also be developed to facilitate standardized data capture and practical adoption of the reporting recommendations.

title: Alberta Quality Assessment Tool for Human Evaluation Studies of Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Question-Answering (QA) Systems: Reporting Checklist
text:
There has been a surge in research exploring the performance of large language models (LLMs) in answering questions within the medical domain. However, the quality of these studies varies significantly, making it challenging to draw reliable conclusions from the existing body of literature. While several quality assessment tools, such as reporting checklists and risk-of-bias frameworks, are available, they are not well-suited for evaluating studies focused on the human evaluation of LLM-based question-and-answer systems. These tools often fail to address the specific challenges and nuances involved in assessing LLM performance in medical contexts.
To address this gap, we aim to develop the Alberta Quality Assessment Tool (AQAT), a reporting checklist specifically for studies that evaluate LLM-based question-answer systems. The AQAT will ensure transparency and completeness in the documentation of LLM evaluations.
The scope of the AQAT will extend beyond general evaluation metrics, incorporating specific factors pertaining to question source, reference answers, evaluator selection, outcome domains and metrics, model explainability, and the generalizability of findings. By creating a dedicated tool for assessing studies on LLM-based systems, we aim to improve the reliability and reproducibility of research in this rapidly evolving field. Ultimately, the AQAT will enable researchers and healthcare professionals to critically assess the performance of LLMs, ensuring that only transparent and reproducible high-quality studies inform decisions related to their deployment.

text:

title: FAIR Omics Reporting for Meta-Analysis
text:
Selecting FAIR-compliant omics studies for meta-analysis is essential to ensure the integrity, reproducibility, and utility of integrated biomedical research. The FAIR principles—Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable—provide a framework for identifying high-quality datasets that can be reliably reused across studies. In the context of omics research, which includes genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and microbiome data, adherence to these principles is critical due to the complexity and volume of data involved.
A standardized reporting framework ensures that only datasets with well-documented clinical metadata, ethical approvals, and appropriate data formats are selected. This enhances data transparency and allows for meaningful cross-study comparisons. Clear eligibility criteria help filter out incomplete or non-human studies, ensuring the data’s relevance to clinical questions. Defined search strategies and data sources make the selection process replicable and reduce bias.
Furthermore, robust data extraction and quality checks support valid statistical integration of heterogeneous omics platforms. Ensuring FAIR compliance also facilitates long-term reuse, contributing to open science and accelerating discoveries. Ultimately, using a structured, FAIR-aligned approach enables meta-analyses that yield clinically actionable insights, minimizes research waste, and strengthens the credibility of systematic reviews in precision medicine.

text:

title: CANGARU - ChatGPT and Artificial Intelligence Natural Large Language Models for Accountable Reporting and Use Guidelines
text:
The CANGARU checklist aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the use of ChatGPT and large language models (LLMs) in healthcare and scientific research and its impact on scientific writing. ChatGPT has gained attention in the medical and scientific community since its launch in December 2022 as a potential tool for decreasing workload while maintaining the workflow. However, its use has raised concerns about its impact on the integrity of scientific literature. CANGARU will focus on standardising the reporting of methods and results for clinical and scientific studies using ChatGPT and other LLMs. The tool will list the most relevant technical details a data scientist needs to report for future reproducibility.
The group developing CANGARU, including representatives from EQUATOR, COPE and editorial members of biomedical and scientific leading journals will conduct a systematic review of the literature, already-registered in the PROSPERO database (CDR: CRD42023406875). The topics identified will be ranked through a Delphi exercise, and after that a team of experts will evaluate the guideline. The panel will include scientists, clinicians, researchers, statisticians, computer scientists, engineers, methodologists, and journal editors. The group plans to publish the reporting guideline in March 2024 as an open-access document, later translated to Spanish, French and Chinese.

title: PLOT (Protocol Lab for Online Trials)
text:
The PLOT consortium aims to build a research reporting checklist for protocols of randomised controlled trials involving the online participation of patients and citizens. PLOT is designed as an extension of the SPIRIT reporting guideline but focussed on the reporting of patient and public involvement (PPI) in trials conducted through the internet. The checklist will apply to clinical trials and also to mixed methods study protocols.
The group has reviewed the literature on patient and public involvement in the design of clinical trials, about the engagement of citizens in clinical trials through online sources and about dissemination practices about PPI. They are also identifying uncertainties around informed consent.
An online Delphi process will be used to develop the reporting guideline to be used in writing protocols for clinical trials involving self-recruitment. This process involves a wide range of stakeholders: researchers, clinicians, patient and public representatives, guideline developers, publishers, epidemiologists, methodologists, ethicists, content experts, funders, journal editors. The PLOT research reporting guideline will be piloted with student groups, new career researchers, contributors for English as a second language, and members of the public (planned for mid-2020). The group plans to publish the PLOT reporting guideline as an open-access document in the last quarter of 2021.
There is a dissemination plan for PLOT involving a dedicated website, the inclusion in the EQUATOR database, publishing editorials, lobbying with journals, academic institutions and funders, presentations in conferences, posting in social media, and online training.

Next, the generated reporting standards will be evaluated in a Delphi process to reach consensus on the guideline items. title: GUIDE-AI - Reporting Checklist on the use of Artificial Inteligence in the Health Guideline Enterprise
text:
In the specific context of the guideline enterprise, AI may support the planning, development and adaptation, reporting, implementation, impact evaluation, certification and appraisal stages. For example, AI tools have the potential of (i) supporting the analysis and synthesis of evidence necessary for the formulation of recommendations, (ii) supporting the assessment of the certainty of evidence, (iii) generating output complementary to that of guideline panel members on question generation, or (iv) improving the quality of dissemination materials and tailoring them to different target audiences. However, there is a need for standardisation and transparency in the reporting of the use of these AI tools and processes. The developers therefore plan to produce a reporting guideline for reporting of AI use in the whole guideline entreprise (from the planning of guidelines to their implementation and evaluation).
The group plan to conduct (i) a scoping review on the use and reporting of AI tools in the guideline enterprise, (ii) draft reporting items based on gathered information, (iii) compare reporting items attained with Guidelines International Network (GIN) extension checklist on use of AI in the guideline enterprise and add relevant subjects and items, (iv) meet with relevant stakeholders (v) evaluate the relative importance of the reporting checklist items and vote on those relevant to the reporting of AI use and (vi) write a manuscript and explanation and elaboration document for publication in a scientific journal.
Work on the project began in June 2024 and the group plan to publish the new guideline as an open access document.

title: PHENOMOVE: Phenotyping standards for reporting signs and symptoms in movement disorders
text:
PHENOMOVE is a reporting guideline under development intended to improve the completeness, consistency, and transparency of clinical phenotype reporting in scientific articles describing people with movement disorders. It will apply to case reports, case series, family studies, genetic or mutational reports, research letters, and observational studies in which movement-disorder signs and symptoms constitute a component. It focuses on the clinical phenotype portion of a manuscript rather than prescribing how a study should be designed or reported in its entirety.
The guideline will include a common set of demographic and clinical items and phenotype-specific modules for parkinsonism, dystonia, hereditary spastic paraplegia, ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, and paroxysmal movement disorders. The modules address onset, anatomical distribution, disease course, relevant motor and non-motor manifestations, associated neurological and systemic features, treatment response, functional milestones, and appropriate rating instruments. They will prompt authors to indicate whether relevant features were reported for all, some, or none of the described participants.
PHENOMOVE is needed because systematic evidence synthesis and experience extracting data for movement-disorder genetic databases, such as MDSGene, have demonstrated frequent omission of clinically important phenotypic information. When a feature is not mentioned, readers cannot distinguish whether it was absent, not assessed, or simply not reported. This limits genotype–phenotype analyses, comparison across studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical interpretation. Existing general guidelines such as CARE and STROBE, and broader phenotype guidance such as PHELIX for ultra-rare genetic conditions, do not provide detailed movement-disorder-specific modules. PHENOMOVE is intended to complement, not replace, those guidelines. It is not a clinical practice guideline, diagnostic tool, research-conduct guideline, or methodological quality-appraisal instrument.

title: TIDieR‑aqua: Template for the Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) for reporting of aquatic interventions
text:
Aquatic therapy/exercise is widely used intervention for diverse populations. It offers unique therapeutic benefits due to the physical properties of water, such as buoyancy, viscosity, hydrostatic pressure, and thermal effects. However, despite a growing body of research on aquatic interventions, studies often lack sufficient detail to allow replication, clinical implementation, or meaningful comparison between trials. This hinders the translation of evidence into practice and limits the inclusion of aquatic therapy studies in systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
Currently, there is no reporting guideline specifically designed for aquatic therapy interventions. While the original TIDieR (Template for Intervention Description and Replication) checklist is a valuable tool for improving the quality of intervention reporting, it does not adequately capture critical components unique to aquatic settings. These include environmental factors (e.g., water depth and temperature), therapist positioning, equipment use in water, safety procedures, and the influence of hydrodynamic forces on movement. As a result, published studies often omit key contextual and procedural details that are essential for replication and for understanding intervention effects.
The TIDieR-aqua considerations are being planned to be developed to fill this gap. It will adapt and extend the original TIDieR checklist to reflect the specific requirements of aquatic therapy. Its aim is to support researchers in providing complete and transparent descriptions of their interventions, ensuring that all critical information is reported consistently across studies. This will facilitate replication, improve intervention fidelity, enhance the interpretation of study findings, and strengthen the evidence base for aquatic studies.

title: Standardised Reporting of the Carbon Footprint of Clinical Pathways
text:
The objective of this guideline is to improve the quality and comprehensiveness of reporting on the carbon emissions associated with clinical care pathways, in particular, the reporting of pathways with a component of remote care, often facilitated by the use of digital technologies.
The development started in January 2024, led by a group from Leeds Teaching Hospitals Trust and Brighton and Sussex Medical School. They clarify that the difference between their project and another already under development, ECoHealth, is that ECoHealth is looking to evaluating products in healthcare, whereas this new project will cover pathways. They argue there is a need to “standardise what components are included in measuring the carbon footprint of a clinical pathway. That will include the products, medications, clinical appointments etc in that pathway.”
A Steering Group has been formed, aiming to produce a preliminary checklist by the end of 2024, to be published by 2026.

section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: Defining Group Care Programs: An Index of Reporting Standards
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

Additional Information


Objective of the STARD initiative
The objective of the STARD initiative is to improve the completeness and transparency of reporting of studies of diagnostic accuracy, to allow readers to assess the potential for bias in the study (internal validity) and to evaluate its generalisability (external validity).

April 2014: The STARD Group and the EQUATOR Network are working together to enhance the information available on this website about the STARD guideline and initiative.

November 2014: The STARD Group is working to update the STARD guideline. A consensus meeting was held in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, in September 2014 and a first draft updated checklist was prepared. Those interested in the process can contact the STARD initiative for more details.

October 2015: The updated STARD 2015 guideline was published.

section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.

Writing manuscripts

Learn more »






Checking

Learn more »

title: Methods and processes of developing the strengthening the reporting of observational studies in epidemiology – veterinary (STROBE-Vet) statement
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.

Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.

title: Clinician-informed explainable artificial intelligence evaluation checklist with metrics (CLIX-M) for AI-powered clinical decision support systems
section: Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
text:
Reporting guidelines are recommendations to help write up research clearly.
Your research will be used by people from different disciplines and backgrounds for decades to come. Reporting guidelines are community-created recommendations for describing what you did and what you found so that everyone can understand, repeat, apply, and synthesise your work. Although they recommend information to include in your manuscript, they don’t dictate how to order that information.
Most reporting guidelines consist of the full guidance (sometimes called an Explanation and Elaboration document) and a checklist. The full guidance provides detailed explanations and examples for each item, and the checklist allows you to demonstrate adherence to editors.
You can use reporting guidelines throughout your research process. However you use reporting guidelines, please cite them.





Writing manuscripts
Write confidently using a reporting guideline to quickly turn a blank page into a thorough and impactful manuscript.

Learn more »






Checking
Use a reporting checklist to demonstrate to an editor or peer reviewer that you have included everything. Many journals require completed checklists at submission.

Learn more »






Writing applications
Reporting guidelines can help you write funding applications, ethics applications, and protocols, but they won’t make design decisions for you!

Learn more »






Reporting guidelines are neither design nor quality appraisal tools.
Although reporting guidelines recommend information to include when writing up research, they do not mandate how to design research. Similarly, when reviewing literature, although you can use reporting guidelines to assess whether a manuscript is well reported, you cannot use them to appraise whether that study is well designed.
